artworks.title: Judgment Tomb — Rhadamanthys (Lefkadia)
artworks.description: In the Judgment Tomb at Lefkadia (ancient Mieza), painted Rhadamanthys stands among the underworld judges — Aeacus, Minos, and the Cretan son of Zeus who rules the Elysian plain in Homer and Plato. Macedonian funerary art makes the righteous judge a door-guardian of the afterlife.

artworks.title: Tomb of the Judgement — Rhadamanthys
artworks.description: A closer view of the Lefkadia Judgment Tomb figure identified as Rhadamanthys — the Cretan lawgiver turned judge of the dead. The painted panel is among the clearest ancient portraits of the triad that weighs souls.

artworks.title: Charon & Cerberus, the Parcae, Minos, Rada & Aeacus, the Eumenides
artworks.description: Hogarth's plate for William King's Pantheon gathers the underworld court: Minos, Rhadamanthus ('Rada'), and Aeacus among Fates and Furies. Eighteenth-century English mythography keeps the Cretan judge in the standard triad of the dead.

artworks.title: Die Unterwelt
artworks.description: Mack's underworld composition places the judges of the dead at the centre of a Romantic hellscape — Rhadamanthus among the classical court that still structures Western images of posthumous judgment.

popCulture.title: Odyssey
popCulture.creator: Homer
popCulture.description: Homer places Rhadamanthus in Elysium — the fairest place on earth where golden-haired Rhadamanthus rules, the Cretan lawgiver as lord of the blessed dead.

popCulture.title: Rhadamanthus
popCulture.description: With Minos and Aeacus, the triad of underworld judges — Plato, Virgil, and later Dante's tradition keep the son of Zeus and Europa as the righteous court of the dead.
